title: Twelve names (Mark 3:7–19)
hookLine: he calls twelve to be with him and to be sent, including the one who'll betray him

cards: By now the crowds are enormous. Mark lists where they come from: Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, the desert country to the south, across the Jordan, even the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon.

So many that Jesus asks for a small boat to stand by, in case he's crushed on the shore. And right then, at the height of it, he walks away. He goes up into the hills and calls a handful of people by name.
Not the biggest donors or the best speakers. Fishermen. A tax collector.
A man who'll one day hand him over.

teach.h: TO BE WITH HIM, THEN TO BE SENT.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "And he ordained twelve, that they should be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach." Two jobs, in that order. First, to be with him.

The Greek for one who is sent is apostolos, where English gets apostle. So an apostle isn't first a manager or a speaker; in Mark, it's someone who has been with Jesus before being sent anywhere. Why twelve?

Israel had twelve tribes, and some readers hear Jesus gathering a renewed people around him, one for each tribe. Then Mark reads out the names, like a roll call. Simon, whom he names Peter, which means rock.

James and John, the sons of Zebedee, whom he nicknames "Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder." Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, another James, Thaddaeus, another Simon, called the Zealot or the Canaanite.

And the last name comes with a note nobody would put in a founding document: "Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him." Mark tells you before you've grown attached. Jesus chose him anyway, and kept him close to the end.

teach.h: A ROLL CALL THAT ENDS WITH JUDAS.
teach.b: That closes a week in Mark: a man with leprosy, touched; four friends through a roof; Levi's table; new wine; grain on the sabbath; a withered hand; and now twelve names, first called to be with him.

how: Christians honor the twelve apostles, and many churches keep feast days for them through the year; Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches describe their bishops as standing in succession from the apostles, while many Protestant churches speak of being apostolic by holding to the apostles' teaching.

games.q: you're Jesus. crowds are coming from every direction and you need help. how do you choose?
o: pick the most gifted speakers in the crowd.
go up into the hills and call the ones you want by name.
let the crowd vote on twelve leaders.
games.why: he goes up the mountain and calls whom he would: fishermen, a tax collector, and Judas, first of all to be with him.

practice: Let names come, one at a time, like a roll call of twelve people who shaped you: a parent or grandparent, a teacher, a friend from a hard year, someone who hurt you and taught you something anyway, someone whose name you've forgotten but whose kindness you haven't.
Don't rank them; if you get stuck, wait, and one more will come. If you pray, thank God for each name.

wordCard.voice: Apostle. From the Greek apostolos, one who is sent. In Mark, called first to be with him, then sent.

orig.note: Greek: one who is sent, from apostellō, to send away. It gives English apostle.

carryVoice: Your line: first, to be with him. The sending can come later. See you tomorrow.
